strengths: The paper addresses a practically important NLP problem: forecasting pretraining loss early enough to guide decisions on the target model. Modeling loss by token position provides an interpretable empirical perspective, and the equations make the proposed pipeline understandable.

The evaluation includes genuine future-loss prediction from training prefixes, beyond retrospective curve fitting. Figures 3 and 5 show substantial improvements over the three tested functional baselines across 468M, 1.2B, and 6.7B models on both ID and OOD validation data. Additional architecture and dataset experiments strengthen the descriptive evidence.

The data-mixture application evaluates completed training runs and downstream performance. The selected mixtures improve all four reported perplexity comparisons and 12 of 14 benchmark comparisons, providing promising evidence of practical utility.
weaknesses: The decisive methodological gap is that the comparisons do not isolate the benefit of token-position decomposition. The proposed predictor incorporates the known cosine learning-rate schedule and a flexible piecewise model, while the aggregate-loss baselines lack those advantages. After the separation point, Equation 10 itself reduces to a cosine plus a constant. A matched aggregate-loss baseline using the same schedule information and functional family is needed to establish the claimed source of improvement.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful configuration tables and pseudocode. The outlier-removal threshold, nonlinear fitting initialization and constraints, evaluation interval, and actual mixture candidates and selected weights are unspecified. Algorithm 1, lines 29–30, also reverses the calibration condition described in Section 2.4: calibration should use observations after the separation point. These details matter for reproducing early extrapolation, particularly without an accompanying implementation or machine-readable trajectories.

The hyperparameter-selection evidence does not establish reliable candidate ranking. Selection uses 10B of 400B tokens, or 2.5%, whereas the forecasting evaluation starts at 10%. Candidate-level predicted and final losses are not reported, so the reliability of this longer extrapolation and the quality of the selected candidate relative to all five alternatives remain unclear. The perplexity gains are modest, and no uncertainty estimates or independent-run variation are reported; averaging the last five checkpoints does not establish robustness.

The claimed generic temporal law is broader than the demonstrated scope. Training uses the Pile and cosine schedules throughout. OOD evaluation does not test robustness to different training distributions or schedules, and the GPT-NeoX/MoE extensions demonstrate fitted trajectories rather than future-loss prediction. The supported contribution should be framed as an empirical predictor under the tested training conditions.

The theoretical interpretations overreach. Appendix C rejects exponential decay after setting its additive offset to zero, although a shifted exponential can approach a positive loss floor. Equation 17 follows from manually freezing two fitted parameters; it does not independently establish that uniform token weighting is preferable. Figure 11 and the three suppression experiments support a limited empirical observation, not the broader conclusion that positional reweighting is unnecessary.

The novelty discussion understates prior work: Kaplan et al. (2020) already analyzes learning curves and loss versus training steps. The contribution should be distinguished through its particular positional decomposition and forecasting procedure, rather than claiming that temporal loss evolution was previously unexplored. Overall, the promising empirical results make this borderline for Findings, but the comparison and reproducibility gaps prevent a clear positive recommendation.
